speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stated in the House on November 5,
1976,	that I would be reporting on my recent talks in Paris regarding Canada-France fisheries questions. I propose to do that today, but first I think it would be useful to review in a more general way developments relating to the implementation of our 200-mile fisheries zone.
The decision to extend our fisheries zones on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts was taken in light of the urgent need to halt the rapid depletion of our fish stocks and arrest the decline of our inshore fisheries industry, a situation which had reached crisis proportions. The urgent nature of this problem required us to take action before conclusion of the Law of the Sea Conference where fisheries questions are among the many matters being discussed. Nevertheless, the new, extended jurisdiction is in conformity with the consensus emerging at the Law of the Sea Conference. The principle is now firmly embodied in the Revised Single Negotiating Text that a coastal state has the sovereign right to manage the living resources of the sea in a 200-mile zone adjacent to its shoreline. The main features of the new Canadian regime are based on the relevant provisions of the Revised Single Negotiating Text.
A number of countries have enacted, or are soon to enact, 200-mile zones, including Mexico, Norway, Denmark, France, the U.K. and the U.S.A. Most recently, the foreign ministers of the Nine agreed that a European Economic Community 200-mile fisheries zone should be in place as of January 1,
1977.	Altogether, there are now some 50 states which have
Fisheries Zones
already, or will soon establish extended Fisheries zones beyond 12 miles, and in many cases as far as 200 miles. Thus, from the standpoint of both emerging treaty law and cumulative state practices there is a sound basis in international law for the action Canada has taken to protect the living resources in waters contiguous to its shoreline.
Canada has not only acted in accordance with emerging international law but has also made every effort to take into account the interests of those states directly affected by our extended jurisdiction. We have been conscious of the need to avoid disputes with other countries stemming from our new fisheries management regime. For this reason, Canada has taken a number of steps, internationally, aimed at achieving a smooth transition to our new 200-mile jurisdiction regime.
Our first priority was to obtain agreement within ICNAF on fishing quotas for the calendar year 1977 which would correspond to Canadian requirements within the 200-mile zone. At Canada's insistence, total allowable catches of stock have been set at levels low enough to ensure rebuilding of threatened species over a period of time. There will be a further meeting of ICNAF in December, in Spain, to deal with the quotas on a few remaining stocks. I should point out for those members who perhaps are not familiar with the shorthand title of ICNAF that it is the International Commission for North Atlantic Fisheries.
The commission, at our urging, is in the process of examining the role it might play in future. We have given formal notice of Canada's intention to withdraw from the convention, as has the U.S.A. I am hopeful, however, that ICNAF can make the necessary adjustment to Canada's exclusive jurisdiction, management and enforcement in the 200-mile zone, and that the new arrangements will preserve the long tradition of international co-operation, particularly in the field of scientific research, which has grown up within the commission. On this basis Canada could continue to play a full and active part in the work of the commission. After the December meeting we will be in a better position to assess what our attitude toward ICNAF should be for the coming year.
Our next priority was to negotiate bilateral agreements with those countries which together account for almost 90 per cent of the foreign fishing operations off our coasts. The government has now concluded an intensive round of bilateral negotiations, and fisheries agreements are now in place with Norway, the U.S.S.R., Poland, Spain and Portugal. These agreements set out the terms and conditions that Canada will apply in permitting foreign fishermen, under Canadian management and control, to harvest certain stocks surplus to our needs.
In addition, we have required the submission of fishing programs from all members of ICNAF who wish to fish off our coasts in 1977. This information is essential in order to ensure that these projected fishing operations are compatible with the quotas established by ICNAF with Canadian concurrence. The problems on the Pacific coast are no less important and we are taking the steps which we consider necessary to ensure that Canadian jurisdiction in our new Pacific zone is

November 19, 1976
Fisheries Zones
effective. Our recent bilateral agreements with the U.S.S.R. and Poland cover the Pacific coast and we are engaging in consultations with other countries that have previously fished there.
The government will also take early action to promulgate an extended fisheries zone in the Arctic. There is no foreign commercial fishing in waters off the Canadian Arctic coast, nor are there depleted stocks requiring urgent conservation measures. However, the government is fully alive to the need to safeguard the fishing interests of the Inuit and to provide for the future development of fisheries in the Arctic area. Consequently, the government has decided to bring into force a 200-mile fisheries zone in the Arctic by March 1, 1977.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:
I have outlined the steps we have taken to ensure a smooth transition to the 200-mile jurisdiction regime. The response has been encouraging. Nations fishing off our coasts have shown a willingness to adapt to the facts of the resource crisis and to the new legal regime which Canada is bringing in.
I now wish to draw the attention of the House to an important aspect of the notice of order in council tabled by my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), on November 2, namely, the geographic co-ordinates defining the fishing zones in which Canada will be exercising jurisdiction. If members agree, 1 would be prepared to table maps prepared by the Canadian hydrographic service illustrating the new zones as prescribed by the co-ordinates in the order in council. That may have to wait until Monday because some of the preparatory work has not been completed. These co-ordinates raise maritime boundary implications with neighbouring countries. The order in council makes express reference to boundary delimitation talks with the U.S., France and Denmark, and affirms that the limits of the Canadian fishing zones as defined in the order are "without prejudice to any negotiations respecting the limits of maritime jurisdiction in such areas."
The United States government has responded to the publication of the order in council by issuing, in the form of a notice in their federal register of November 4, 1976, a list of co-ordinates defining the lateral limits of its prospective fisheries zone, as well as its continental shelf in the areas adjacent to Canada. In a number of areas these lines differ from the Canadian co-ordinates. We do not accept these lines and we are so informing the United States government through diplomatic channels.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:
1 am pleased to note, however, that the U.S. government has mirrored the approach taken in the order in council by making it clear in the federal register notice that the co-ordinates listed therein are without prejudice to any negotiation with Canada or to any positions which may have been or may be adopted respecting the limits of maritime jurisdiction in the boundary areas adjacent to Canada.

During my visit to France I had occasion to discuss with the French foreign minister our plans for extension of jurisdiction by January 1 in the area off our east coast. At that time, precisely on November 3, the European Community officially announced the decision taken by all member countries to extend their jurisdiction over fisheries to 200 miles by January 1, 1977. While the new management regime will be decided by the community, the determination of the exact areas to be brought under extended jurisdiction, of course, continues to belong to the individual member countries, and the matter of delimitation of waters off St. Pierre and Miquelon remains a question for Canada and France to work out.
What I particularly wished to underline in Paris-and my French colleague was quick to respond favourably-relates to the urgent need for both our countries to put in place by the end of this year interim arrangements in waters close to the French islands. Such arrangements would avoid conflicting fisheries regulations on matters such as enforcement and licensing. I am confident that as a result of those discussions in Paris, both sides have a keener appreciation of the necessity of early agreement on these agreements.
Interim arrangements are especially necessary in the absence of agreed maritime boundaries off the coasts of the French islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon. While France has given itself enabling legislation to extend jurisdiction off any of its coasts, there has been no indication to date by France of its intentions regarding the area off St. Pierre and Miquelon. In the preamble to the order in council extending jurisdiction, we clearly indicated that the establishment of an extended fishing zone is not intended to prejudice ongoing consultations on the delimitation of waters with France, and this matter is also being pursued.
Another important factor in our fisheries relations with France is that the bilateral fisheries agreement concluded in 1972 grants certain rights to French vessels and in particular, to vessels registered in St. Pierre and Miquelon in the areas that are now under Canadian jurisdiction, that is, in our 12-mile territorial sea and in the Gulf. These rights, which are not modified by the creation of our new zones, were granted in exchange for the abandonment by France of important treaty rights in extensive areas dating back to the time of French settlement in the area. Similar rights were granted to Canadian vessels off the coast of St. Pierre and Miquelon. We have made very clear to the French that the rights granted to their vessels by this agreement are exclusive to France, and cannot in any way be claimed or exercised by other members of the European Community.
The 1972 bilateral agreement also refers to the possibility of extension by either country. In article 2, the agreement states that each country will, in the event of a modification of the areas under its jurisdiction, undertake on the basis of reciprocity to recognize the right of nationals of the other country to continue to fish in the modified areas, under rules and regulations to be applied by the country having jurisdiction,
November 19, 1976

including, in our view, regulations on quotas, licensing and enforcement.
In making this statement today, I should like, with your permission, sir, to extend a word of appreciation to my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment for his very active participation in all these discussions over a prolonged period, and to compliment him on the successful negotiations of bilateral treaties with the countries 1 have mentioned.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext: I think it is entirely appropriate, also, to add a word of commendation to the officials in the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Fisheries and the Environment who, by unanimous agreement, are some of the best-informed and skilled people in this field anywhere in the world and who, I believe, have done a most creditable job for this country, as I am sure they will continue to do.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened with interest to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) covering the extension of our fishing zones. I wish to thank him for making the statement available to the official opposition prior to its presentation in the House.
The statement makes it clear that the decision to extend our fisheries zones on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts was taken in light of the rapid depletion of our fish stocks, creating a situation of crisis proportions. However, the decline in our fisheries resources is not something which has occurred recently. Rather, it is a situation which has been brought about because of excessive overfishing by foreign nationals operating on our continental shelf over a long period of time. It was this overfishing which brought about the first Law of the Sea Conference in 1958 followed by subsequent conferences in 1960 and 1974 in Caracas, in 1975 in Geneva, and in New York in 1976. The crime of the century, as far as our fishing industry is concerned, is that the knowledge gained from all these conferences and all the contacts made with representatives of other governments has not yet led to a suitable agreement for the over-all management of our fish stocks.
The minister stated, "Our first priority was to obtain agreement within ICNAF on fishing quotas for the calendar year 1977 which would correspond to Canadian requirements within the 200-mile zone." The minister is surely aware that ICNAF, like the quotas it has established over the years, has been a dismal failure. This paternal organization and its associated scientists have carried out a tremendous amount of useful work. However, it now appears that the greed of nations which motivated the quotas, or "numbers game", worked the system to the disadvantage of everyone.
National quotas for fish have been juggled, and international deceit has created what our fishermen call "paper fish", resulting in a tremendous waste of effort in negotiations
Fisheries Zones
between nations for certain species of fish which they have virtually wiped out. Then at this late date, after all these negotiations, all the minister can tell us is that 1977 quotas for catches in our 200-mile zone are based on quotas established by ICNAF, an organization which is everywhere discredited because of its inefficiency and lack of control over incidental catches.
These are not my views alone. The Minister of Fisheries, in his proposed management plan for the Atlantic groundfish fishery in 1977, puts forward the view that next year the prospects facing the industry are even more dismal. This is due to those ICNAF quotas. He states that the Gulf redfish stock continues to deteriorate. He points out that on the Scotian shelf the greatest declines have occurred in stocks of cod and pollock, from 30,000 tons to 7,000 tons and from 55,000 tons to 30,000 tons respectively. In summary, the highest possible catch the Canadian fleet could take, according to the minister, is 85,730 tons, which is 3,000 tons less than last year on the Scotian shelf. These are the fruits of ICNAF as they apply to Atlantic Canada, and since we account for only 7 per cent of the total fishing tonnage off our coasts taken by ships in excess of 50 tons, it is obvious that Canadians play a very small part in overfishing any species.
The minister went on to tell us that bilateral agreements have been negotiated with those countries which together account for almost 90 per cent of foreign fishing operations off our coasts, and that agreements are now in place with Norway, the U.S.S.R., Poland, Spain and Portugal. What about Japan? What about Korea, East Germany, Cuba and other fishing nations? What tonnage will they take next year? It is these bilateral agreements which are today causing such concern to the Canadian fishing industry. I say to members opposite, through you, Mr. Speaker, "You have, in effect, given away the key to our fishing banks, and our fishing banks are just as important as our chartered banks".
The minister's generosity to foreign nations in 1977 will do nothing for Canada or for our fisheries resources. According to his own figures, there are no fish surplus to the needs of Canadians in 1977, but this fact was not recognized by his officials at ICNAF. Canadians have only been allocated 17.5 per cent of the cod catch, 6 per cent of the mackerel and 23 per cent of the redfish. In contrast, Mr. Speaker, Russia, which has consistently overfished our resources, is rewarded by ICNAF with 13 per cent of the cod catch, 33 per cent of the mackerel and 50.4 per cent of the redfish.

My colleague asks, what about the capelin? The food fish and the codfish have been given away by this government to the Russians. The minister's bilateral agreements, which were supposed to be a breakthrough, represent, instead, the outright selling of Atlantic Canada's birthright. That is what he has done. We on this side cannot applaud a policy which continues to permit foreign overfishing while

November 19, 1976
Fisheries Zones
Canadians remain at home and Canadian fishermen are forced to draw unemployment insurance. Unfortunately, those who work in our fish plants are unable to draw unemployment insurance due to the sporadic nature of their employment. They may work on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and because they are laid off for two or three days in the week those in the plants, due to government policies, are unfortunately unable to earn any money or draw unemployment insurance.
This is the situation that now applies to our fishermen in many of our ICNAF areas. We are told that next year's quotas will be even less than the quotas for 1976. This type of discrimination will not be tolerated by our people. The situation our fishermen face today is a far cry from the flowing picture painted by government supporters of the benefits which would accrue to Canadians from a 200-mile limit.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the minister indicated that he would be prepared to table maps illustrating the new zones, even though agreement on these co-ordinates has not been reached with the United States, France and Denmark. It is a matter of some regret that this government, after attending numerous Law of the Sea Conferences, is at this late date unable to lay down boundary lines in agreement with out maritime neighbours. The best that the minister can promise is interim agreements with France and the United States on major problem areas of vital concern to Atlantic Canada, especially to our fishermen in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia.
Obviously, the government's efforts in the field of international diplomacy have been no more successful than their efforts in dealing with the economy, unemployment and inflation. They have all been a dismal failure. The high hopes of Canadian fishermen for a better future and bigger catches under a 200-mile limit must now be tempered with the sad fact that this government does not intend to permit Canadians freely to fish in their own waters, a ruling that cannot help put create massive social problems in our coastal areas.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement, if read very carefully, referred to the Canada-France fisheries question. I have read through that part of the statement dealing with this question and, to put it mildly, it is extremely vague, full of hopes and is lacking any particular substance. Nevertheless, I think both the minister and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) deserve congratulations on the progress made in various fields toward protecting fishing stocks in Canadian waters, or what will be Canadian waters.
The preservation of our fisheries is, as we all know in this House, of vital importance to the people of Canada, especially on the east and west coasts. It is also important to all of us from an economic and human point of view. The minister referred to "crisis proportions" and the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) used exactly the same expression. I am prepared to make it unanimous on behalf of this party and say we also recognize the crisis proportions which have been reached in regard to the protection of our fisheries.

Initially, Mr. Speaker, we would have been of the view that it would have been preferable to wait for the proposed extension of our fishing jurisdiction and its declaration until the Law of the Sea Conference had reached a general agreement, and presumably have the benefit of universality under the auspices of the United Nations. Nevertheless, we recognize that it was just not possible to wait that long and we welcome the fact that the government is moving ahead. I think it is on January 1, 1977, that our declaration of the expanded fishing zones becomes law and enforceable by Canada. Although we are nationalists, we do believe in a degree of international support, both in the revised single negotiating text and a series of bilateral agreements. We feel we are justified in moving out ahead of, instead of waiting for, the universal agreement that we hope will come.
We must recognize that there are extremely serious gaps in the minister's statement. First of all, I want to refer to what is essential to any policy, namely, an adequate means of enforcement. I suggest that this statement indicates, once again, the necessity for those responsible for defence in this country to look at what our priorities should be. I think that protection of our sovereign waters as extended should be one of the very highest priorities in defence matters. This would mean building more ships and increasing the number of patrols.
It is no good laying down laws, drawing lines on maps and calling them zones, and so on, unless you have every intention of enforcing those zones and are in a position to do so. This may require a change in priorities. For example, I think that we needed a long-range patrol aircraft to go all the way across the Atlantic to destroy mythical submarines like we needed a hole in the head. Here we have something relevant to our needs which has to be done, but I am afraid that by spending $1 billion on the wrong thing we may not be ready to spend enough on the right things in the field of defence which are essential to the welfare of our people.
There are, as the minister's statement made clear, other serious gaps. There is the question of defining the co-ordinates; I do not know whether I am translating that correctly when I call it fixing the boundaries of the fishing zones. We still have to reach agreement with the United States on that matter. We also have differences with France. All we have heard from the minister is that the French are understanding and are ready to discuss the matter.
I am pleased to see that in regard to some of the interim agreements they will perhaps be ready to deal with them before the end of the year. This is an item of unfinished business. It may be that negotiation can fill the gap and make it possible to apply these zones effectively without international dispute. It may be that we will have in some cases to go to arbitration or even to the International Court to settle a dispute.
Mr. Speaker, as has already been mentioned, there are serious gaps in regard to countries such as Japan which are immensely important in this field, particularly as it affects our
November 19, 1976

west coast offshore. My understanding is that the northern pacific treaty is due to expire before very long. When that happens, it is of the utmost importance that we have in place an adequate agreement on this matter with Japan.
To summarize what we would say in regard to this matter: The statement is vague, but some of the things it says are clearly moving in the right direction and we welcome them. There are serious gaps, however, particularly in regard to enforcing it. I suppose this is fair enough if it is a matter for the Department of National Defence, but it is clearly related to this whole program. We urge the government to proceed with all dispatch to close some of those gaps so that these immensely important resources of our fisheries may be preserved, not only for the benefit of our own people but for the benefit of others to whom this is a highly important source of nutrition.

As a comment on the minister's statement, even if Canada could do more to protect our fisheries, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) deserves our congratulations for his considerable effort to protect that important Canadian industry. 1 am especially pleased with the decision to extend the territorial zone to 200 miles, even during an important conference on the law of the sea. I am convinced that if my colleague the member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) were in the House, he could comment more knowledgeably on that statement since he is the member of our party who has been specifically asked to consider the matter.
However, I am glad that at long last Canada has acted as a sovereign country. This attitude may spur other countries to do so. According to the statement, there will be another conference in December and 1 hope that the good intentions mentioned in the statement will be maintained at the forthcoming conference and that once again Canada will assert itself, not to the prejudice of other countries, but to really protect our industry and allow our fishermen to earn their living honourably. We recall that several years ago fishermen had a hard time. Action taken by both federal and provincial governments made it possible to improve their lot. We must not quit now, we must go forward much faster if we really want to maintain and improve our fishing industry.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very glad to answer the hon. member's question, and I thank him for his kind references. On November 3, the European Economic Community indicated that all nine countries would accept a so-called 200-mile territorial zone. It is up to each individual country, however, to decide which portions of its coastal waters, or all of them, it is going to include in that 200 miles. To the best of our information and knowledge at the moment, nothing has been said by the nine countries as yet about what they propose to do individually.
In theory, of course, the situation in St. Pierre and Miquelon is, as the hon. member said, that it is part of France. Therefore, setting aside altogether what the European Economic Community does, France unilaterally, obviously, has the right to define what it considers to be its 200 miles. However-and this is the point that I believe the hon. member is getting at- it then, other than in that sector, cannot have the European Economic Community agreement transcend its treaty with Canada. We have made it very clear to them that since 1972 there is a treaty between Canada and France. The French government cannot now say, in effect, to the EEC that because the nine have agreed on a 200-mile zone which the community will totally use, that agreement supersedes the agreement it has with Canada.

November 19, 1976
Fisheries Zones
The best legal advice we have is that it would not be possible, for instance, for non-fishing nations, in terms of ones that have never fished in the North Atlantic or any category of that kind, to come in under the umbrella of the EEC agreement. It is still basically a Canada-France agreement and we would have total negotiating control over it.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister and I grew up with a background of this kind of history and the treaty of Utrecht which we were studying while our Canadian counterparts were studying the British North America Act. I say that to the minister because my understanding is that that treaty is still very much binding both on Canada and France.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree this is a matter which we both studied a long time ago, but I fear I am a little hazy on the treaty of Utrecht at the moment. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:

If that was the thrust of the original question, that has been done. In so far as the 200 miles is concerned, it is described, as I recall it, in the single negotiating text as a 12-mile territorial sea and 188 miles of economic zone. I gather the question was whether we would go beyond 200 miles. There is no thought at the moment of going beyond 200 miles by any country, to the best of my knowledge.
The continuing importance of ICNAF which was mentioned relates to the fact that there are stocks beyond the 200 miles which will still have to be managed and which are migratory over the 200-mile line. On the sectoral approach, I would ask the hon. member to bear with me, because obviously we are in the midst of discussions on that subject and I think it would be advisable not to say anything publicly in that regard.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have now before the House Bill C-22, to amend the Income Tax Act, arising out of the budget of May 25. The purpose of the bill, as hon. members know, is to implement a number of the important changes in taxation provisions affecting individuals which were introduced in that budget, as well as some changes in the corporation tax and, in particular, a change in the general tax regime dealing with charities under the Income Tax Act and a change in the definition and mode of operation of charities as dealt with in the Income Tax Act.
Naturally, at second reading I would want to discuss those specific amendments, but before doing so, in response to the undertaking I gave to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) on Wednesday, I would like to comment on the economic and fiscal situation as we see it at the present time in light of changes which have occurred in the nearly six months which have intervened since the statement was made on the evening of May 25. It would be useful to recall the very grave dangers which faced the Canadian economy in the autumn of 1975, and the comprehensive program of action we announced on October 14, 1975. At that time we set the goal of achieving a gradual reduction in the rate of inflation which was threatening the very foundations of our social and economic progress. At the same time we looked toward a moderate pace of recovery in terms of growing output and employment.
The objective we set for slowing the rate of inflation was rather specific. It was to bring down the year over year rate of increase in the consumer price index from 10.6 per cent in October, 1975, to 8 per cent in October, 1976, and by a further 2 per cent per year thereafter. As the House knows, that target of reduction of the rate of inflation was not only achieved but was, indeed, overachieved in the time-frame. The consumer price index in October was only 6.2 per cent above its level a year earlier, and Canadian consumers have benefited from lower food prices. I think it is important to emphasize, as we look at the perspective of dealing with inflation in the coming 12-month period, that the beneficial effects, for example, of a drop in food prices which have been passed on by way of lower food costs for consumers cannot be expected to continue for the next 12-month period. If it is our wish that our farmers should continue to be able to keep on producing economically and producing to meet Canadian needs, we will have to expect that returns at the farm gate will improve somewhat over those of recent months.
Still looking at the persepective of the economy as a whole, there can be no doubt that there has been a marked slowing in the inflationary tide. The result of this has been a major gain

in the purchasing power of workers' takehome pay, even though the rate of increase in dollar wage settlements-that is to say, in nominal terms-is only half what it was a year ago. Nevertheless, we have a long way to go before we are out of a situation of danger with regard to inflation in Canada. Our costs in Canada are still rising faster than those in the United States, and while it is true that inflationary expectations may have been dampened in this country, I do not believe they have been sufficiently turned around to ensure the continuing health of the economy.
May I now turn from the question of inflation to estimates of growth. At the time of the budget I anticipated that real growth in 1976 would be at the level of about 5 per cent, and that unemployment would continue at the recent trend level, which at that time was just above 7 per cent, and that there would be a gradual decline as cyclical expansion both in Canada and in our trading partners took hold. It now looks as if there may be a small shortfall from that 5 per cent real growth which we had anticipated on May 25.
It is, of course, difficult at the best of times to predict what that rate is going to be with fine precision. It is all the more difficult to predict it this afternoon when we have not yet received figures concerning the performance of the Canadian economy in the third quarter of 1976; we have not received the most relevant, recent figures from which we can attempt to make some predictions in the several quarters ahead. Having said that, I confirm again that we expect a shortfall below that 5 per cent level which I had set out in the May 25 budget, but the shortfall, given the relatively satisfactory performance, particularly in the first quarter of 1976, should be not too far below the 5 per cent level.
The rate of unemployment is, and continues to be, a matter of general concern. The rate continues to be influenced by erratic month to month movements which reflect work stoppages. I am referring, for example, to collective bargaining situations and other factors which are relatively temporary. I remind hon. members that when we consider figures which became known last week with the publication of the October figures, we are looking at a situation in which the rate of unemployment has come down substantially in British Columbia from the rates which had been experienced several months previously. These figures reflect not inconsiderably the fact that extensive work stoppages which that province had been undergoing during the summer of 1976 had been brought to an end and there has been a substantial return of working people to employment, along with some cyclical growth brought on by the expansion of exports.
In the same way, when looking at figures for last month, we note in particular the impact on Ontario figures of the strike at the Ford Motor Company which had rippled effects throughout the Canadian economy or the part of the economy in that part of the country which had to do with the auto pact. There was, therefore, an impact on employment in the Ontario area and for that reason unemployment was up in that area.
November 19, 1976

It now seems clear that the rate of unemployment in the last quarter of 1976, that is to say, the present-day period, will average somewhat more than the trend level indicated in the May budget. As I recall-if I may refer to the May budget- we were at that time looking at a rate of 7.2 per cent; we are looking at a rate, in the month of October, of 7.6 per cent, or a variation upward of between 7 per cent and 8 per cent over figures anticipated for the fall of 1976. This continues to be a matter of concern.
What is of particular concern is that because of our commitment to restrain government expenditures in support of the anti-inflation program the flexibility previously available to the government for dealing with unemployment, for example by substantial expansion in government expenditures, is simply not present. Indeed, if one looks at expenditures in the economy over-all, one will notice not only the restraint of expenditures at the federal level but also the restraint of expenditures at other levels of government, this reflecting the fiscal stringency which all economic levels in this country face.
Therefore, the government sector has not been providing the stimulus to the economy which has been the experience in past years. This is the result, on the one hand, of our success in dealing with the levels of government expenditure in Canada, but the cost must be paid on the other side in terms of the lack of stimulating effect by the government on economic activity in the country. My colleagues and I continue to keep the unemployment situation under the closest attention. In particular, while we are concerned about unemployment rates in all parts of Canada and, if I may add parenthetically, particularly unemployment rates among those in the 17 to 24-year age group, we are particularly concerned about regional unemployment levels in the Atlantic provinces and Quebec which are higher than the Canadian average and have increased most rapidly in recent months.
As I have indicated, and as hon. members know, the tempo of expansion slowed in recent months not only in Canada but also in the United States and other industrialized countries- countries with whom we trade in a major way and whose performance is measured along with ours in the figures of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. It now appears likely that the growth performance of the OECD group as a whole, which includes Canada, in the year 1976 will fall short of the 5.5 per cent forecast set out in the economic outlook paper of that organization which was published in July and formed the basis of the declaration of policy guidelines agreed upon at the summit meeting of major economic countries at Puerto Rico.
At that time, ministers and chief executives laid considerable emphasis on the impact of inflation on western economies as a whole and the necessity for restraint of inflation measures which would bring corresponding benefits in terms of lower rates of cost increases. Indeed, some in the private sector, writers on editorial pages and economic commentators, have wondered whether, in light of the sorry performance of the OECD as a whole, it is not incumbent on some of the major countries of the OECD group-that is to say, the United
Income Tax
States, Japan and major countries in the European Economic Community-to engage at this time in more stimulative measures than were contemplated when the prime ministers and ministers met in Puerto Rico.
Turning to our balance of trade and the prospect of slower growth in the countries which are our major trading partners, our balance has improved this year but we cannot but be unaffected by the slower growth which has occurred in our trading partners. This is a matter of concern. The sustained health of the Canadian economy depends on further reducing the large current account deficit, that is to say, the current account deficit on our balance of payments as opposed to the balance of trade, and it also depends on a substantial upturn in capital investment.
Perhaps I could refer hon. members back to the remarks I had occasion to make in the throne speech debate with regard to the capital investment climate in OECD countries as a whole. I suggested that economic commentators had drawn attention to the caution being exercised in all major countries, or at least to caution respecting declaration of investment intentions if not to the commencement of investment at this point in the economic cycle. The observation had been made that in these countries as a whole investment was not occurring as rapidly as had occurred in past cycles, reflecting perhaps the caution induced upon investors in all countries because of the traumatic shock they had been through, particularly because of the levels of recession in previous months.
I would like to comment briefly on the government's fiscal position. In some ways it is a corollary to the comments I made earlier about the impact of government spending on the economy as a whole. At this stage, from estimates of expenditure, I can report that our persistent efforts to restrain additional expenditure are bearing fruit. We are confident we can meet our target as set out at the time of the budget in total outlays this year of $42,150 million. Indeed, we feel we have won some room for flexibility in terms of our spending programs. We are in the process of considering a possible redirection of some of those fiscal resources into areas that would respond to the needs of the economy, particularly the concern I cited with regard to regional unemployment and unemployment among certain constituent groups in the work force.
My colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), will be announcing to the House very shortly some redirection of spending in relation to employment programs, programs which have been selected on a number of criteria. First, of course, they should be targeted particularly for those groups where there have been high rates of unemployment; and, second, programs which can start producing an impact on unemployment right away this winter rather than measures similar to taxation measures which could have a longer term macroeconomic effect, but no effect this winter. Because my colleague will be making a statement within the next ten days or so, 1 will not go further into the details except to say that we anticipate being able to apply additional public

November 19, 1976
Income Tax
funds for the support of direct employment measures this winter.
Looking at the other side of the government balance sheet, that is to say, at the question of revenues, one of the corollaries of a slower rate of growth is that the rate of growth of revenues of the government of Canada has been slower than was anticipated at the time of the budget statement. Revenues, therefore, appear to be falling somewhat short of those projected at the time of the budget. The consequence is that I now expect our financial requirements, excluding foreign exchange transactions, may amount to a little over $5 billion in this current fiscal year, compared with the $4'/2 billion which 1 forecast on budget night in May.
I have made reference to some of the principal economic concerns: to inflation, the rate of growth in the economy, levels of employment, the government's efforts to restrain the growth of expenditure, our revenue projections and, finally, the impact of all these factors on the government's cash balance. I hope to be able to keep the House advised as time goes on of any discernible efforts we have made in this regard. In the short term we will be concentrating our efforts in the next several months on the problem of unemployment, particularly, as I have said, on the specific target groups. In summary, we are ahead of the track we set for ourselves with regard to inflation, but are somewhat behind where we had expected to be in terms of output and employment. In connection with employment, we are keeping a very close eye on the situation. 1 hardly need to empahsize the uncertainties there are at the present time, not only with regard to economic problems here in Canada but in the world at large.
Perhaps I can take occasion to repeat here in the House a point which I had occasion to lay some stress on outside the House. That is with regard to the potential impact on Canada and the rest of the industrial world, and indeed on the world economy generally, of the much discussed potential increase in price by OPEC countries for crude oil sold abroad. There could be little argument with the fact that at this point in the economic cycle of the industrial countries the recovery from recession has not been so robust that a substantial increase in an industrial cost, such as for energy, would not have a rather great impact upon the recovery. The wise counsel that we hope the OPEC ministers will take is that a substantial increase in the price of oil internationally at this time, or indeed any increase in price in oil at this time, could put in jeopardy the economic recovery which is so important not only to the prosperity of the industrial countries but the developing countries as well. Therefore, a restraint from a price increase on January 1, 1977, would be of widespread interest.
I will not confine myself to special pleading on the part of Canada or, indeed, all industrial countries in this regard. We and other representatives of OECD have shown a capacity to protect ourselves substantially from the impact of an oil price increase. The community which has suffered most, and indeed is not yet out of the difficulties created by past increases, is that group of non-oil producing developing countries. That is one of the principal concerns we have had in terms of our

development assistance program. For the industrial countries, this involves a slower economic growth and slower recovery from the recession. When an oil price increase is translated to the non-oil producing developing countries, it pushes them very close to the edge of survival in terms of the state of their economy and in terms of the health and safety of their population. Because of the shaky growth in the industrial world and the impact on non-oil producing developing countries, a restraint on oil price increases would be wise counsel for the OPEC countries at this time.
Coming back to Canada, I emphasize again that we would not hesitate to make whatever mid-course directions seem appropriate in terms of directing the Canadian economy. In doing so, we have to recognize at all times that we have set ourselves a very narrow framework in which to make the changes. Above all, we must try to avoid swinging violently between "stop" and "go". We must not forget that the one essential condition for restoring the health of the Canadian economy is continued success on the anti-inflation front.
I now wish to refer to the specific amendments to the tax law which are put forward in the bill. Members will have noted in reading the bill that a number of significant amendments of a relieving nature are being put forward affecting the income of individuals. For example, at a cost this year of $15 million in revenues I have introduced a measure which for 1976 and subsequent years effectively doubles the deductions permitted working women and single parent fathers in respect of their child-care expenses. The maximum amount will now be limited to the least of $4,000, $1,000 per child and two-thirds of the taxpayers' earned income for the year. Also, for 1976 and subsequent years, taxpayer parents of a disabled dependent child will be able to deduct any portion of their child's disability deduction which cannot be used in relation to deduction from the income of the child itself.
Moving to the other end of the life spectrum, to assist taxpayers in saving for their retirement the bill provides for substantial increases in the maximum annual contribution limits for registered retirement savings plans, registered pension plans and deferred profit sharing plans. For example, an individual who is not a member of a company pension plan may, for 1976 and later years, contribute up to $5,500 per year to his registered retirement savings plan. The previous maximum was $4,000. Commencing also in this taxation year, an employee and his employer may each contribute a yearly maximum of $3,500 to a registered pension plan on the employee's behalf. The previous limit was $2,500. Similarly, the employer contribution to a deferred profit sharing plan is increased to a permissible $3,500 annually from $2,500. Also, in respect of deferred income plans the rules governing registered home ownership savings plans will be amended to permit taxpayers to shift plans from one institution to another should they decide to do so. The increases in contribution limits for deferred income plans mean that taxpayers as a whole will be able to save an additional $60 million annually which would otherwise have gone to pay taxes.
November 19, 1976

The present bill also includes provisions to establish a simplified mechanism for calculating the amount of deductions which may be transferred between spouses, including the age exemption, the investment income deduction, the pension deduction, the disability deduction and the student living allowance. Relieving provisions are introduced to ensure the deductibility of certain expenses incurred by taxpayers living abroad, to amend the principal residence rules relating to divorced or separated individuals and spouses of transferred employees, and to amend certain capital gains provisions relating to estates and trusts. A number of other provisions respecting individuals are included to simplify existing tax treatment, to cure anomalies and prevent unintended results.
Mr. Speaker, the bill also gives expression to a number of important measures announced in my May budget relating to corporate taxpayers. A measure of substantial benefit to incorporated small businesses which played such a prominent role in our economy involves a further major increase in small business deduction limits. Effective for 1976 and subsequent taxation years, the maximum annual amount of the active business income of Canadian-controlled private corporations subject to the 25 per cent low rate will be increased from $100,000 to $150,000 and the total accumulative limit will be increased from $500,000 to $750,000. Canadian small business will save an additional $30 million in taxes in the first full year as a result of this measure.
Deadlines have been extended and rules modified to provide relief when taxpayers elect to pay dividends out of various corporate surplus accounts. The taxpayer's ability to object and appeal various determinations made by the Minister of National Revenue has been broadened. In addition, certain modifications have been made with respect to the tax treatment of life insurance companies, foreign affiliates and nonresident corporations.
The culmination of one of the major efforts in the review of the tax system is recognized, as well. Members will recall that the budget referred to certain conclusions and proposed changes resulting from an intensive review of the capital cost allowance system. Our system was found to be basically sound and in line with the tax depreciation systems of other industrial countries while possessing relative advantages in terms of certainty and simplicity. Some changes in rates were indicated, however, and these were described in the budget papers. Since the budget I have received a number of representations by taxpayers affected by these proposed changes. Regulations making the necessary rate adjustments have resulted from this additional input and are due to be published shortly. Regulations providing for a basic change in capital cost allowance rules respecting leased and moveable property have already been published.
Also in this context of capital allowance I should like to take this opportunity to announce that I have decided to extend for a further year the two-year, fast write-off on equipment designed to control water and air pollution. This incentive rate would otherwise have expired at the end of the year.
Income Tax
Mr. Speaker, let me turn briefly, now, to the subject of resource taxation. In recent years, federal and provincial governments have been obliged to make some hard decisions concerning fiscal arrangements for the petroleum and mining industry. Conscious of the need to maintain the stability of the tax system which has now evolved, I am not proposing any major changes in this area.
It is important, however, that Canadians be encouraged to invest funds in resource exploration. To encourage vital exploration activity, the bill proposes that all taxpayers, whether individuals or corporations, be allowed an immediate 100 per cent deduction with respect to Canadian expenses incurred after May 25, 1976, and before July 1, 1979. Deductions in respect of such expenses were previously limited to 30 per cent per annum for individuals and corporations whose principal business was outside the resource industries. The incentive period is to be limited to three years to allow the government the benefit of a trial period in which to assess the utility of this measure in terms of the stimulus to extra exploration.
Before leaving this subject, I should like to commend recent provincial initiatives aimed at encouraging taxpayers to seek out new reserves or maximize recoverability of existing reserves. In this regard, the bill contains an amendment making it clear that provincial government incentives such as the drilling incentive credits provided by Alberta and Saskatchewan will not reduce a taxpayer's potential deductions in respect of Canadian exploration or development expenses.
An equally important side of our over-all national resource policy is energy conservation. Members will recall that my May budget made reference to a number of incentives and deterrents designed to promote energy conservation. One important incentive involves the expansion of the present two-year, fast write-off to include certain types of equipment acquired after May 25, 1976, and before 1980 which contribute to the efficient use of energy resources. Regulations pertaining to this measure have already been published.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words concerning the taxation of charities. In the May budget I announced a set of proposals involving changes in the Income Tax Act having to do with the definition and operation of charities. These proposals stem from a discussion paper tabled along with the June, 1975, budget, from more than 200 briefs, from many oral representations prompted by the discussion paper and from an intensive study conducted by the government. The proposed changes in income tax are designed to promote public confidence in, and support for, charitable activities while at the same time ensuring that tax exempt moneys flowing to charities are used as intended for strictly charitable purposes and not for private gain. The new rules seek to do this in a number of ways: by rationalizing the classification of charities; by enforcing minimum annual levels of distributions for charitable purposes by charitable foundations enjoying tax advantages; by limiting excessive fund-raising costs, and by requiring a greater degree of public disclo-

sure of the finances and charitable activities of all registered charities.
1 do not need to persuade members of the importance of charitable activities in Canada. The growth and development of charitable institutions and activities has been most significant in recent years and the changes proposed represent a comprehensive effort to modernize tax laws and further the public interest in this area.
I have outlined in general terms, Mr. Speaker, the more important tax proposals contained in the bill. Hon. members will be examining the detailed provisions effecting these measures as well as the other relatively minor changes of a technical nature which are included in the bill as we proceed, in committee of the whole, to examine the bill on a clause by clause basis. I will be happy to provide any further explanation and elaboration which members may require to enable them to support these measures when they are put to a final vote.

Mr. Speaker, before referring more specifically to some of the provisions of Bill C-22, I should like on behalf of my colleagues and other members of the House to say we are very pleased that the minister has given to a certain extent a state of confederation speech respecting various matters of an economic nature. I am particularly pleased the minister has done this in response to the request made by the members of my party, particularly by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), who asked that such a statement be made.
Perhaps I will be allowed to make some comments concerning some of the observations made by the minister. Speaking very generally, although I think he was reasonably frank in his remarks I felt there was very little sense of urgency regarding the terrible plight of our business community at the present time. As I recall, Mr. Speaker, the minister dealt, for example, with inflation, indicating that he felt the initial target of an 8 per cent level had been more than met in that in October the rate, compared to the rate the year before, was about 6.2 per cent. The minister mentioned that food prices had been a very significant contributor to that relatively low level of 6.2 per cent. I certainly agree with the minister that in all likelihood food prices are going to start bumping back and that the favourable cost of living level so far as food prices are concerned will not continue.
I should like to emphasize that it is somewhat misleading when the minister takes credit at this juncture for inflation being at 6.2 per cent compared to a year ago and does not comment on the fact that in the last three months inflation actually seems to be on the rise again. In the last three months, on an annual basis, inflation is over 8 per cent, not 6.2 per cent, comparing month by month with a year ago.
In touching on the loss of purchasing power, the minister stated that purchasing power among employees was coming back, that it had risen. Mr. Speaker, I would hope it has. The fact is that the real earnings of employees in Canada declined

by something like $200 between the years 1972 and 1975. If the minister is indicating that his figures reveal that this purchasing power is now starting to come back, then it is about time the government gave the House this information.
Dealing with real growth, I was disappointed to hear the minister state that he felt the estimate he made in his may budget of a growth of about 5 per cent is not likely to be attained. Those who recall the budget debate will remember that we on this side of the House stated that the 5 per cent target which the minister had set was too low, that realistically it should have been a real growth target of 6 per cent. At that time we felt the minister had deliberately shot too low at 5 per cent in the earnest hope that he could exceed it and look well. Now to be told by the minister that the rather low target of 5 per cent growth is not going to be attained is most alarming.
I say it is most alarming because, when we suggested a 6 per cent real growth, we did so in the context of realizing that in 1975 and in 1974 there had been a drop in real growth in the aggregate of 7 per cent below potential. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, this is why we have over 200,000 extra Canadians out of work today. The fundamental lack of real growth of the kind the economy is capable of represents a failure on the part of the government.
I am rather fascinated by how the government's attitude shifts so quickly from telling us that their problems are of an international nature, then of a domestic nature, and then back again to an international nature. How many of us in this House recall that when we suggested the imposition of wage and price controls in the period 1973-74 and the imposition of a restrained fiscal posture and monetary posture, the government told us that this would not work because the problems we were having to live with were of an international nature.
We do not believe that this is true, Mr. Speaker. We believe that essentially the government failed to move at the time that they should have moved. We then found that when it suited their purpose, and in anticipation of bringing in the wage and price controls program, they said that, to and behold, international conditions were not the problem and they shifted back to the argument that the problems were domestic ones and that wage and price controls may have some effect. Today we find, the government's having not attained the relatively low goal in real growth of 5 per cent, that they tell us that it is not their fault, that again the problem is an international one, and the government quote figures from OECD and other convenient figures that they can find among foreign countries.
This is not being responsible, Mr. Speaker. The fact is that the government must accept responsibility for the sad performance of our economy. I am disappointed at the lack of leadership shown for so many years, not only by this minister but by his predecessor, leadership that is apparently not going to be provided if we can judge from the remarks of the minister today.
When the minister dealt with unemployment, he said he had hoped in his budget that unemployment would follow what he called the recent trend line, but that he now feels that it looks as if it is going to fall short of that. I was startled to hear him
November 19, 1976

say that unemployment will range between 7 and 8 per cent in the fall of 1976. If 8 per cent is actually the level, this will mean 800,000 Canadians are needlessly out of work because of a misfiring budget that was brought down in May of this year.
It is not only the sad fact that 800,000 people will be out of work, Mr. Speaker. We must also bear in mind that, according to the latest figures, 30 per cent of those out of work have been out of work for 14 weeks or longer. With figures getting that high, we are getting to chronic, hard-core unemployment. Mr. Speaker, I will deal with this question more fully when I deal with Bill C-22 more specifically, but I believe that hon. members should be reminded of the suggestions we made in May on the budgetary position with respect to what this economy needs. We said we felt there was room to slash about SI billion from the spending estimates that the minister has confirmed today were excessive. We suggested that the money should be used first of all to give Canadian taxpayers a substantial tax cut and, secondly, to reduce the deficit that the minister indicated today will be about half a billion dollars higher than the figure he suggested last May. I am pleased that some of my colleagues on my left are now suggesting tax cuts, Mr. Speaker. Even they have caught on to the fact that it might be wise to stimulate this economy, and that what the minister proposed last May was inadequate.
If I could return to what the minister said today, he just glanced-and I use the word advisedly-at this country's trade problem. He said that the balance of trade has improved. It is misleading to say that our balance of trade has improved without making two or three things clear. First, the current account deficit has not improved in this country. Second, the reason the balance of trade has improved is not so much that manufactured articles have been exported but that raw resources are being exported at an ever-growing rate. The hard fact is that there is almost a $10 billion deficit in manufactured goods as far as our trade position is concerned. For the minister to suggest that merchandise which includes all other articles-wheat, livestock, raw resources, etc.-is in surplus is not being candid without pointing out the dire circumstances that our manufactured export goods are in vis-a-vis the import of several manufactured goods.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that every trade account today, other than resources, is in deficit. Our tourist trade deficit is about $1 billion and the invisibles, such as interest, dividends and royalties, are greatly in deficit and will be every month, bearing in mind the amount of foreign money we are borrowing, literally, to pay for consumption in this country. This government is allowing the nation to act like a family that is paying for every day's food by credit card. But there will be a day of reckoning, and hopefully this party will be in power and will be able to do something about it.

As the minister knows, he is not in a position to reply to the various questions I would like to put to him at this time. It is important to consider Bill C-22 in its proper context. That context basically is in relation to the budget we referred to of last May. Bill C-22 is the most important piece of legislation that will arise from the budget. As a piece of legislation it will be one of the most important bills that will come before this House, certainly this year, and possibly for an even longer period. As we know it is a highly technical type of legislation. I believe most agree it can be dealt with best in committee of the whole.
I believe there are significant aspects of the legislation that deserve comment in an over-view sense, and in fact in the over-view sense that the minister has already entered into in his general remarks concerning the state of the economy. I suggest there were no fresh ideas in the May budget that was introduced. Then, as now, there was no new perspective, long-range or otherwise, that would give Canadians a renewed hope in their future, that would give them hope that our staggering levels of jobless will find employment, hope that our real growth will regain what we lost in the sad years of 1974 and 1975, and that we are losing even in real growth in the

current year. There is no hope that we will regain our position in per capita national wealth among the nations of the world, and there is no hope that our $5 billion current trade deficit will not be even higher than anticipated in May.
Even now as we have learned that an economic recovery has not materialized as the minister predicted in his budget, even now as our real growth stagnates, even now as an additional 50,000 jobless swell our unemployment rolls to a disgraceful three quarters of a million Canadians, even now as the minister repeatedly rejects requests from this House to address himself to our worsening economic position which has rendered his budget clearly out of date, which in many ways means that this bill should be amended, even now when the minister's message is clear-"economy heal thyself' he says- is it any wonder that the non-budget of last May is here represented by 105 pages of the most ho-hum income tax legislation this House will see for some time?
The combined effect of proposed tariff and taxation legislation as indicated by the minister in his budget speech is a net reduction in budgetary revenues of $75 million during our current fiscal year. The minister today made certain comments about the losses of revenue in respect of income tax cut-backs and I point out that he was speaking only in relatively small terms, tens of millions of dollars. We will again propose measures today, as we did last May, that will slash revenue from taxes by more than three times the amount suggested by the minister. One proposal alone, designed to provide an incentive to small businesses, would result in a savings equal to that of the tax and tariff measures combined which the minister announced last May. Our concept of a tax cut to stimulate growth in the sector where it is needed most, the private sector where jobs and national wealth are created, is a concept which has been gaining currency throughout the land since we introduced it six months ago.
The Institute for Policy Analysis in a release on November 2 entitled "Time for Tax Reduction" stated that sluggish economic growth and higher unemployment rates are in the cards unless the government acts soon to revive the flagging private domestic sector. The Institute proposes a fiscal package which includes a 5 per cent across-the-board tax cut in personal income taxes, and a 5 per cent investment tax credit. If such a program were implemented the result, the Institute claims, would be a halt in the rise of unemployment rates early next year at V/i per cent instead of the projected 8 per cent. Perhaps in anticipation of the minister's continuing insistence that inflation, and inflation alone, remains the primary target, the report argues that "the effects of the tax reduction program on the rate of price inflation appear negligible".
I am encouraged by that report. I believe the government, particularly the Minister of Finance, should read it and, instead of confirming that unemployment will go up to 8 per cent, why does he not seriously consider our suggestion of last May of a tax cut to stimulate the economy, and allow that unemployment level to be at least more moderate than he expects?

Yes, and the New Democratic Party which is always slow on these things has discovered that tax cuts would be in order. The simple fact is that the government always seems to be about a year behind our advice. Unfortunately the circumstances had changed and they did it at a time when they should not have done what they did, namely, bring in a program that would have been more suitable about 12 or 15 months earlier. Now they appear to be doing exactly the same thing. They brought in a budget which we suggested should have contained more tax cuts. They declined to bring in those tax cuts. Now, six months later, they still decline to give those tax cuts. They may do so six months from now, but that may be too late to avoid the type of economic behaviour we are talking about today.
Wood Gundy Limited is also among those who favour stimulating the economy through tax cuts. In a forecast published in October of 1976 that firm examines two alternative scenarios for the Canadian economy through 1978. What are the results? The first scenario is that if we rely on a sluggish upturn in the U.S. economy-which I suggest is the essential feature of the May budget-our export volume will increase by only 3.9 per cent and 4.3 per cent in 1977 and 1978, instead of 7.5 per cent and 5.7 per cent. The Wood Gundy report states in addition that the trade deficit will actually climb to around $6 billion.
If I may, I should like to quote what Wood Gundy predicts, as follows:
The domestic economy would weaken rapidly, real consumer spending growth would slow to only 2 per cent in 1977 and we predict no real growth in business capital spending in 1977.
The real gross national product in this scenario will rise by less than 1.5 per cent in 1977. This is the urgency of what we are facing, and yet 1 sense a strange complacency on the part of the minister. Somehow he is bound and he cannot move, and yet more and more economists are saying that he must move, that he made a mistake, and that he should move for the benefit of those who deserve better than to be without work in this fine country of ours.
I would also point out that a tax cut in all likelihood would lower our trade deficit. The Wood Gundy figures anticipate an approximate tax cut of 3 per cent, while the proposal we put to the House last May recommended about this same amount so far as the personal income tax cut is concerned. Finally, the Wood Gundy report states:
We do not believe that the rate of inflation would be significantly worsened in 1977 or 1978 by such a tax cut policy.
In short, we can continue hopefully to improve our inflation performance, and I would even suggest that if we could make up our mind to disband the Anti-Inflation Board this would allow inflation to go down quicker than is the case at present. That is the silly thing about the present government stance.
Income Tax
We have a relatively high level of inflation, certainly higher than in the United States, and at the same time our unemployment levels are totally unacceptable. Surely the answer is to regulate the economy in the form of business regulations, to allow those who wish to invest to get on with job creation in this country, to do their job, and to get the economy rolling.
Let us look at our proposal which we brought before the House six months ago when, incidentally, we predicted an increase of 50,000 jobless as a result of the budgetary measures brought in by the minister, and I would recommend that hon. members read Hansard. We ask hon. members to bear this proposal in mind when they consider the various aspects of Bill C-22.
The tax cut favoured by my party is based on possible savings of $1,025 million, and that was what we thought could and should have been saved. Today I emphasize again that the minister has indicated he will not go over the $42.1 billion level as he said in May, but now he admits they have some leaway, some possible expenditures which they can re-route and, as I said before, that is a nice way of saving when they have a little too much money and they are trying to figure out where to spend it. Let us give it back, as we suggested, in part to the Canadian taxpayer. For the sake of brevity I will not now repeat the figures for the savings, but I should like to refer hon. members to pages 13895 to 13900 of Hansard of May 27 for a detailed explanation of the program which we felt at that time could be brought in to save Canadian taxpayers some money.
Of the $1 billion we proposed to save we suggested that a tax break of $250 million should have been given to the Canadian taxpayer who is increasingly paying the shot for this administration's mismanagement. Hon. members should not forget that aggregate personal income taxes based on the May budget were anticipated to jump 26 per cent this year alone over last year. In 1968, the year the Prime Minister took office, personal income taxes represented 34 per cent of the total revenue received by Ottawa, while corporate taxation represented 15 per cent. Today personal income taxes supply an amazing 53 per cent of Ottawa's take, while the corporate sector still accounts for that 15 per cent. In short, it is not the fat-cat, the wealthy, or the vague corporate entity which pays; in the main it is the average hard working Canadian who shoulders this wasteful and ineffective administration's costs.
We suggest, as we did last May, a 10 per cent tax credit, which would be about $100 million for those earning $8,000 or less. The remaining $150 million of our tax approach would have been given in credits scaled down appropriately in relation to those earning between $8,000 and $16,000.
We believed, and we still believe it is time to give the taxpayers such a break for three very good reasons: first, the real gross national product per employee in Canada, as I have indicated, actually went down by $200 since 1972 compared to 1975. In 1975 the average employee earned $11,645 in real dollars compared with $11,848 in 1972. Surely it is wrong to deny a tax break to such employees who are being required to restrain their wage increases.
