Second, as we have pointed out, this administration will reap a bonanza in personal income tax aggregate increases which this year will total $3.3 billion. An 8 per cent reduction in this tremendous bonanza, as we suggested, would not appear to be out of line.
Third and most important, the government has confirmed to the minister today that it does not need the money which we budgeted for last May.
There are other measures as well which we believed in May would stimulate the economy and provide the jobs and growth that are lacking in the country. Once again I would refer hon. members to Hansard of May 27 for details on our $100 million incentive to the private sector to encourage it in the expansion of its research and development activities. We also suggested that there should be a $75 million plan to encourage export sales, especially in the case of small businesses. I emphasize that both would have been simply financed out of the $1 billion savings that we felt could have been made in the spending estimates which were put before us last May.
As I indicated earlier, the provisions of this bill are rather detailed and I would remind hon. members that my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), will be dealing with most of these provisions extensively. This is a fairly technical bill which contains 105 pages and 86 clauses of tax amendments, and surely most comments on these sections should be best left to the committee of the whole stage during which my colleagues and I will have much to say about individual provisions.
One thing which is perhaps overlooked is the question of the withholding tax on corporate and provincial bond issues. As I am sure hon. members are aware, the withholding tax on corporate bond issues was lifted on June 23, 1975, and the same tax had been lifted earlier, on April 15, 1966, as far as provincial bond issues were concerned. Unless there is a change in legislation, both taxes, as I understand it, are to be reinstated in 1979. As we have noted before in this House, the result of this action has been the rapid growth of foreign debt financing, from zero in the second quarter of 1975 to nearly $7 billion through September of this year. Not only has the holding tax been removed, but this government has also embarked on strange interest structuring, and as of today the prime lending rate in Canada is a full 4 per cent higher than in the United States.
Morgan Guaranty Trust in New York lowered its prime rate today to 6'A per cent. In this country we have had a 1014 per cent prime lending rate since March of last year. The Americans have been lowering their rate, which was already in the 6 per cent rage last March. They have been lowering their level, and yet we have had a constant 10 'A per cent rate, which is partly a result of no witholding tax and partly a result of the differential which has resulted from a tremendous inflow of debt capital-and I emphasize debt-to this country which has been used by the government mainly for consumption purposes.

It will require years for us to pay the interest load before we do anything as far as our trade balance is concerned. That is just nuts. It should not happen, yet that is exactly what is happening, and this government has allowed our current account trade deficit to get sharply out of line. Dealing with this I point out that in the second quarter it is anticipated that this will continue, and if I may I would like to refer to the chief economist of the Royal Bank of Canada, Dr. Ralph G. M. Sultan.
Dr. Sultan estimated that in the first quarter of 1976 Canada sustained a net inflow of almost $2.5 billion, or nearly $10 billion at an annual rate, of foreign borrowings. This borrowing in the first three months alone will cost Canadians a tidy sum, nearly, $175 million per year in interest payments, year after year into the foreseeable future. Put another way, this three months of financial cover will cost Canadians each year about two months of their total lumber exports, or about one month of their total wheat exports, or close to one month of their total mining and concentrates exports. Partly because of the suspension of this tax provision Canada accounted for an amazing 46 per cent of all foreign bonds and 22 per cent of all Eurobonds in the first quarter of this year. If we may, we will say more later on this subject.
I would like to touch on capital gains. This party has on repeated occasions called for indexing of the capital gains tax. We have always felt that to exclude this tax from the principle of inflation adjustment, a principle which is widely implemented in many other areas of taxation, is unfair and demonstrates how easily the "soak-the-rich" philosophy backfires, to the detriment of middle income groups.
From information now available from the Department of National Revenue for the first three years since the introduction of a capital gains tax, we now know that the overwhelming majority of taxpayers reporting taxable capital gains earned a total income, including these gains, of less than $25,000. In 1972 and 1973, 86 per cent of those taxed on capital gains were the non wealthy. In 1974 this percentage was 83 per cent. In all three years this middle income group paid between 30 per cent and 40 per cent of the total capital gains tax which was collected by federal authorities. We will be looking more closely at this tax, especially since it now seems possible that this tax may have contributed to the shrinking of the Canadian pool of risk capital so necessary to maintain a growth rate which could reduce unemployment. Moreover, it has already encouraged the export by Canadians of their badly needed investment capital.
Our constituents have also written to us, and undoubtedly to other hon. members of this House, concerning certain clauses dealing with the effects of the Income Tax Act on Ontario farmers, particularly clauses 70, 73 and 80. We will examine this as well at the appropriate time.
In conclusion, I again remind hon. members that as we look at this bill in the coming weeks we will view it for what it surely is: the residual graffiti of a budget which, six months after presentation, has been discredited by some of the most severe economic developments in 15 years. It is in this context
November 19, 1976

that we have offered the House and the country conservative and constructive alternatives.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening very carefully and with great interest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), I feel that I simply have to respond to what the hon. member for York-Simcoe had to say about the choice which is being offered the country. It seems to me, now that capital punishment has been abolished, we have a choice between being drawn or quartered and, as far as I am concerned, that is not much of a choice.
Having listened to both hon. gentleman it seems to me that they both are oblivious to something we must take into account. Both of them are talking about solutions which are disappearing from this world. 1 hate to call upon the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for confirmation of what I am trying to say, but what the Prime Minister said in his speech around Christmas last had a great deal of truth to it. It is unfortunate that he has lost his nerve, or his party has lost its nerve and has not proceeded accordingly.
What I am going to attempt to show in my remarks this afternoon is that both the government and the official opposition are arguing in a vacuum. They are arguing like so many generals. They are fighting the last war rather than seeing that we have a completely new situation facing us in economics, and neither of them seems to be prepared to deal with it.
If we consider past recessions and recoveries, a number of things become evident. I think it is important to take that kind of historical look in order to place what I want to say in perspective. I will deal just with the recent past. I will begin with the ending of the second world war. Much of the prosperity then was based on a pent up consumer demand which had not been filled during the war. We were on a wartime footing, and there was no time to manufacture things like washing machines, tires, or even cars themselves, and for many years we were able to keep the economy going on the residue of savings which had been made during the second world war and the demand for consumer goods.
Following that there were a number of wars, and wars always seem to be good for prosperity, as dreadful as they may be in terms of the human condition. That is the one way the western world has maintained a semblance of prosperity. There was the Korean war and the war in Viet Nam. Then there was the great baby boom. There was growth which stimulated housing, the construction of schools and all kinds of other things, and in between there were great technological advances. There was the advent of television, both black and white, and colour, everything that went with that, and the whole electronic era with all the new gadgets and gimmicks. Cameras also came on to the market, and there was tremendous expansion.
But what is the situation today? I am not going to say that the end of the technological invasion is here; I am sure more advances will be made. A number of things have already
Income Tax
happened. Our society has altered in a very fundamental way, but there are still many people who have not had their needs satisfied. There is still demand for consumer goods, but almost invariably that demand exists among people without money to buy things.
The government encourages those who are reasonably well off to save their money; consequently much money is saved and not spent on consumer goods. The post-war baby boom is largely over, the population growth has started to slow, and the government has reduced the rate of immigration. All these factors contributed in the past to economic growth. This country, the United States, the European Common Market and most other industrialized countries are in the midst of a recession. There can be no doubt about it. We have severe unemployment, and the minister this afternoon did not paint a happy picture of our economy. Our prospects are not cheerful. The question is, how are we to climb out of the recession? We shall need to do something fundamentally different from what has been done previously.
I was sorry to hear the Minister of Finance use strikes as a phony excuse for our high unemployment figures. He tried to say that well, yes, the unemployment figures are high, but some part of the figures, can be attributed to numerous strikes. We know that strikes contribute to unemployment Figures; but even if you took all strikers out of the unemployment figures, or reduced unemployment figures by 100,000 to compensate for people on strike, you would still be left with a horrendously large figure.
A Canadian Press report in one of this afternoon's newspapers shows that the number of job vacancies has dropped in the last three months from 59,700 to about 56,900. When you compare the number of job vacancies with about 679,000 people looking for work, you can see that the picture is dismal. I suppose there was a time one could argue, especially when the job vacancy rate was high, that some people did not want to work. Present day figures show that this is not so. People want to work. The current job vacancy rate takes into account little more than normal seasonal shifts and people changing jobs. What the unemployment figures do not show, and they would be considerably higher if they did, is the number of people who have dropped out of the labour market or are no longer registered as unemployed because they have given up hope of finding a job.
Conditions are changing; I do not know if the government and hon. members to my right are aware of the changes taking place and are prepared to act accordingly. I see no evidence to show that the Minister of Finance is concerned about what is happening and is prepared to make fundamental decisions necessary for correcting unemployment. He will need to act at some point; why he delays I do not know.
As the hon. member for York-Simcoe correctly said, when it suits the government's purposes it will say that a difficulty really is an international problem and we can do nothing about it. The truth is that these are not international difficulties; we

November 19, 1976
Income Tax
are considering a domestic problem and the government must intervene in the economy. Unemployment does not happen in the abstract. True, we are not the only country with unemployment difficulties; other countries experience them as well. When we suffer from inflation, other countries suffer from it as well. Yet surely the government can do certain things to improve conditions in this country. So far this government has done little in this regard.
Let me indicate some of the things which must be taken into account and which are not being considered. First, given unemployment of the dimensions I have outlined, the first priority of any government is to get people back to work. But in his remarks to the House the minister was still beating the anti-inflation drum, saying that inflation is the most serious difficulty we face. I am aware of the existence of inflation; but was not the anti-inflation program established to take care of inflation? Has not the government taken pleasure in pointing out that, in its judgment, inflation has been controlled? If that is the case what argument has it for not expanding the economy right now? Inevitably any system of controls such as brought in by the government will contain elements of unfairness. If there is any justification for such controls it is this: they are to be used as a tool, as an instrument for doing something worth while. That "something worth while" means getting people back to work.
The government must decide if it will encourage resource industries or encourage manufacturing industries. So far the government has always said, "We will encourage both. But you cannot do both. Bill C-22, instead of encouraging manufacturing as it should be doing is offering advantages for resource speculators and encouraging them to get back into the business. Mr. Speaker, we cannot provide jobs for our unemployed merely by encouraging resource industries. We should not encourage resource industries to produce more than we need for our domestic use and for meeting our commitments to foreign nations. Stimulating the resource industries is a losing battle, and by encouraging speculators to return to that field Bill C-22 is waging a losing battle. How many jobs will we create if we bring the speculators back? I suggest that the more resources we export, the higher will be the value of our dollar; this means that we shall bring in increasing quantities of imports in the form of manufactured goods and there will be still fewer jobs in Canada. That is a prescription for continued, chronic unemployment, yet the government persists in that kind of policy.
The government argues that it is encouraging manufacturing industries by giving tax breaks to small businessmen. My friends on my right seem to be of the mistaken view that the tax-break policies they advocate have been echoed by the NDP. Let me make it clear that when we talk about tax breaks we mean something entirely different from what the Conservative party means when it talks about tax breaks. Although the hon. member for York-Simcoe seemed to make his obeisance to fairness by suggesting that his party, if in power, would give tax breaks to people at the lower end of the income scale, he made it clear that most of the money he

would be prepared to forgo in taxes would go to encourage investment, that is, to encourage people in the private sector to speculate. I see the hon. member shaking his head. Surely the whole tenor of his remarks was that he would encourage the private sector to make additional investments in order to get the economy going. I cannot be wrong in that, surely.

speechtext:
Yes, but the hon. member's policy would mean substantial benefits in other areas as well. Both the government and hon. members to my right keep saying that we must stimulate investment, and in the last number of years the government has made substantial concessions in this respect by providing over-generous depreciation allowances to business for capital investment. It has lowered corporate taxes year after year in order to provide business with internal revenues for increasing investment. If one wanted to be cynical one could show that there is an inverse relationship between tax concessions and unemployment. As the government has lowered the business tax rate, unemployment has climbed. That is the only conclusion one can draw.
The point I make is this: There is not any direct relationship between a tax cut, a tax benefit given to business, and the amount of employment created. During the last number of years when the benefits given to business have been of the highest order, we have had the highest levels of unemployment. They just do not go hand in hand.
If you take that kind of argument to its conclusion, you are talking about an international trade war. If one country lowers its corporate tax rate, its competitors are tempted to do the same. In fact the justification for lowering our tax rate was that the Americans had introduced the DISC program and we had to follow suit. It is a losing game, especially when it does not result in employment.
According to existing evidence our problem is not that we are short of capital, capital goods, or that we can get prosperity by encouraging capital investment. The latest figures that I have seen on plant utilization in Canada show that we are limping along at something like 80 per cent of capacity. If there were consumer demand in our society, our present factories could put every single Canadian back to work without additional investment. That is because the rate of utilization at the present time is so low.
This week a friend of mine handed me a paper which I think is important. I argue that even using the standard concept of capital utilization, we are far from using what we now have. We could absorb the unemployed without any real incentives to additional capital formation. There might be some bottlenecks, some things that are not perfect. Some plants may now be operating at 100 per cent capacity while others might only be at 60 per cent. Obviously there are some problems of that kind. However, if the market is good, the demand is good, and taxes are reasonable-not give-away taxes, but reasonable
November 19, 1976

taxes-those industries can respond without the general sort of give-away programs the government has brought into play.
I wish to refer to the paper that was brought to my attention. I ask hon. members not to be frightened by the title, "The Theory of Capital Utilization and Idleness". It appeared in the Journal of Economic Literature, 1974. The author is Gordon C. Winston of Williams College. I read from page 1,301 which I think is the pertinent section. The point Dr. Winston is making is that even though it looks like there is full utilization of capital, most capital remains idle or is not used under the best of circumstances. I quote:
-and more important for the present discussion, the highest level of utilization reached (in 1954) was only a meagre 22.9 per cent of the time ... Put more bluntly, the United States manufacturing capital stock was idle over 75 per cent of the time, even in the best of years.
I realize that I am using a study that was carried out in the United States. However, it is not irrelevant to our discussion. If anything, the figures from a Canadian study would be more startling because, from the information we have, capital utilization in the United States is much better than in Canada. The point that is being made by a statement of that kind is that, when you are into a recession, the problem is not the absence of capital or the equipment, but how you couple demand to existing and potential capacity. That is where the failure has taken place.
Reverting to what I said earlier, the demand, if it is going to take place in the future, is of a different nature than that of the past. I do not see the same kinds of situations that gave relative prosperity in this and other countries following World War II continuing. I do not see that it is going to be coming from the private sector.
If we are going to be prosperous there will need to be greater government intervention, greater planning of our economy. If not, we will be doomed to the abnormal and unconscionable levels of unemployment we are now experiencing and which show every indication of becoming greater and greater as this year goes on. We will have to find a different tax system and a different method of income distribution if we are to succeed.
There was a medieval theory that was popular for many years. If the rich consumed richly, the poor would benefit. It was a very self-serving kind of theory that only the rich believed and only the rich could find evidence to support. In fact for centuries the theory simply was not true. It was simply a justification to support those who were well off against those who were not so well off.
It was not until we got political democracy and the ordinary person had a greater say in the management of the affairs of state that we were able to move toward the prosperity of the twentieth century. That was brought about by mass consumption by the little man, a lot of it because we were able to tax much of the benefits of the better off. That process must continue.
Unless we move to a more egalitarian kind of society and unless we are prepared for a greater redistribution of income, our society cannot be prosperous again. My party certainly
Income Tax
hope we can persuade the Canadian people that redistribution of income and equality of conditions is a good thing. To some extent we have been successful. Perhaps one reason why our argument has been accepted over the years is because it is not only a good thing from a moral point of view, but also from an economic point of view.
If it were not for the present level of redistribution of income through such programs as family allowances, old age pensions, and unemployment insurance, we would be in a much deeper recession. Rather than what we are in now, we would be in a bad depression like we had in the thirties.
If you compare the degree of suffering and hardship in one country against another, let us say the European Common Market and the countries in North America, you will find that the degree of hardship and frustration is almost in direct relationship to how much of a social welfare program those countries have instituted. It is small wonder that some of the greatest hardships being undergone at the present time, in terms of suffering by workers, are being experienced in the United States. Support programs which exist in Canada do not exist in the United States to the same extent. The least amount of suffering is taking place in the Scandinavian countries and Germany where there is an involvement in social democratic ideas.
I am suggesting that we need to find a new base for prosperity, a good base, in my view a moral base, and a much better base than having three quarters of a million people out of work. There are a number of things we could do. There might be tax cuts for people with low incomes-tax credits, rather, because tax cuts tend to help those who are better off rather than those who are worse off. If we really wished to improve the lot of the very poor we could introduce a system of tax credits.

As a further step we should be thinking about providing for earlier retirement. We in this party did come close to persuading many in this House and in the country of the merits of lowering the retirement age for women to age 60. I believe that to some extent women's lib interfered with that, but aside from that I believe the government thought it could get off more cheaply by a formula under which, if one spouse was 65 and retired, and his income did not exceed a certain amount, and the other spouse had reached the age of 60, they would both be eligible. I am sure somebody figured out how grand this would sound to the public and how little it would cost the federal treasury. That is better than nothing at all, and on that basis I shall not denounce the arrangement. But relatively few people can profit from that program. I think there is a great deal to be said not only for lowering the age of retirement to 60 in the case of women but for lowering the retirement age generally to that figure.

Many people have asked me this question, and I am sure they have addressed it to every member of parliament. They say, "I have worked all my life, 1 have worked in the workshops for 35 or 40 years; why should I continue working while 750,000 people need jobs and have to be supported by unemployment insurance benefits; would it not be more decent, more humane for me to retire at an earlier age and give work to young people?" What is the answer to this point of view? It is a perfectly sensible approach. It might be argued that an early retirement program of this kind would cost money. Well, it costs a great deal of money at the present time to support unemployed people. The cost is horrendous. I believe, of course, that the state has an obligation to provide jobs; if the state does not provide jobs it is evidence of failure on the part of the state, because full employment is possible. If it fails to provide jobs, it has an obligation to set up support programs.
A serious characteristic of unemployment, if it persists too long and if support programs continue too long, is that many people become accustomed to being supported and not having to work. This is not good for them, and it is certainly not good for society. As members of a social democratic party we take the view that the state has an obligation to provide jobs in the same sense as people have an obligation to take those jobs. It is the greatest mismanagement of the economy to continue a situation where jobs are not available, and thus increasing numbers of people are inclined to regard living on support programs as a way of life. It is tragic from that point of view, but it is also tragic from the point of view that the money spent could have gone to help people who are poor, people who are old, people who are disadvantaged. While some of those who are supported through unemployment insurance benefits may be poor, and while some of them may be disadvantaged, they are not all in that category. Numbers of them have reasonably high incomes. It is a destruction of any ordinary moral concept that humanity should continue in this way.
There are other things we could do. For example, we need housing for senior citizens. Now is the time we should be building such accommodation. From what I have been able to see, the senior citizens' housing we have built so far has been of good quality and highly acceptable. We should be increasing the amounts paid to the disabled, to those who are no longer capable of forming part of the labour force. It would be much better for society to pay the money out in that direction. It would not be saved. That money would be spent on goods and services and it would provide employment for those who are now unemployed.
We should be increasing family allowances. If we look at the statistics on poverty we find that one of the great causes of poverty is that people have children when their incomes are not sufficient to look after those children. The market system does not care about the responsibilities of a father or mother in terms of the number of children they have to look after. The market system pays the same rate for a young single man as for a man or woman with family responsibilities. In an age in which standards of living are improving, it is only just that we

should redistribute income through family allowances. It is better to do it that way than through other programs.
If we lower the age of retirement, if we improve family allowances, if we start to construct the things we need, both now and in the future, we shall be able to put people back to work. We shall not be able to do it any other way. We do not want to start wars. I would prefer to live this way, or even worse, than see prosperity brought on through war.
To judge from the government's attitude to immigration we cannot expect in future to see a continuation of the waves of immigration which in the past provided much of the impetus for development, much of the demand for housing and consumer goods.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, a special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be appointed to consider the advisability of taking an initiative in seeking to promote closer relations with the former British possessions in the West Indies, such as the Turks and Caicos Islands, which have not yet attained independence, and further that if the residents of any of these islands so desire it, economic and political union of these islands with the Dominion of Canada be negotiated at an early date at the proper constitutional levels.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is not a new proposal for me. In fact the general area has been of great interest to me since I came to this House, as it was indeed of interest to me in the misty era before I arrived.
In the years following Confederation the Dominion of Canada was limited in its control of its foreign policy. Our international outlook never really got beyond the United Kingdom and the United States. But as we matured and moved beyond our total absorption with our relations with these powers, our first meaningful contacts were with the area then described as the British West Indies.
In 1885 Sir John A. Macdonald appointed Sir Francis Hincks, former governor of Barbados, as his adviser on West Indian affairs. In 1889-1890 Sir George Foster, Macdonald's finance minister, visited the area. A preliminary conference was held in Barbados in 1890. Later a royal commission was set up including two ministers of the Laurier government. In 1912 the first Canada-West Indies conference was held in Ottawa. In 1920 another conference convened in our capital,
West Indies
and another in 1925. From these flowed special trade and tariff arrangements. One might say that the last in the conference series was that of 1966 presided over by our late Prime Minister and leading internationalist, the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson.
Thus it is in our historic tradition that I advance a plea for special consideration for our southern commonwealth neighbours. It is not inappropriate that today's motion should come from a member representing a part of Atlantic Canada. Our people had close commercial ties and warm relations with the Caribbean community long before Confederation. If I may mingle my commodities if not mix my metaphors, this was in the golden age of wooden ships and iron men. I am glad that my seconder is also from Atlantic Canada because he knows the value of the ties which bound our two regions together, for we sold them codfish and brought back rum, and probably got the better part of the bargain, nutritionists' views to the contrary notwithstanding.
In those days our ocean-side position was a stimulus to commerce and not a barrier, as in these days of exorbitant freight rates, user pay policies, and other harassments of the geographic extremities of this country.
I gave some thought to rewording my motion since the Turks and Caicos matter is not now so timely as it was two or three years ago, but I refrained from deleting this portion lest I be seen to agree in any way with the cold, callous statement made by the government on April 10, 1974. I found this statement paternalistic in the extreme, suggesting that the residents of these little islands really didn't know their own best interests. 1 also found it somewhat difficult to accept the logic that anything which financially favoured small communities and not more populous neighbours would be wrong. Surely we do not, for instance, adopt in our Cl DA programming the notion that, unless we can universalize our efforts, we do nothing.
It may well be that there has been a great diminution of interest on the part of the people of the Turks and Caicos Islands in any kind of special association with Canada. But, apart from union, this country could have done much more to help those very small islands. In this connection I have made representations to former ministers and to the president of CIDA, but I regret to say without too much success.
There is a tendency today to leave human problems to vast world bodies. Too often one gets the feeling that if we can just construct the proper, elaborate international agency, the gap between the developed and developing world will disappear. Of course, we must improve our international concepts and programs, but there will still be a vital area for bilateral arrangements and we must never overlook the special responsibility which special opportunities provide.
I have always believed that with the Commonwealth Caribbean we have both. We also have special ties, and I hope a special interest. Those who cherish the British parliamentary tradition should note the progress and process of development of the small political communities in the Commonwealth Caribbean. Some have moved to full independence and have
80005-9>/2

November 19, 1976
West Indies
taken their place in the Commonwealth, the U.N. and other world bodies. Often in the face of great disadvantages they have built viable economies. More important still is the development of their political institutions. With certain exceptional deviations, the parliamentary structure has developed and flourished. I have often been impressed by the manner in which veritable mini-states have been able to make the parliamentary system work. It is a credit to the people and, with a certain partiality, I would say to the system also.
The main purpose of my motion is to indicate to the people of the Commonwealth Caribbean that our parliament and our people still regard them as very special friends and that, without seeking to intrude upon their judgments on their own future development, we are ready to discuss with them helpfully and cordially any matters up to and including a closer association in the economic or political sphere.
In a debate in an earlier session on this motion I was accused of being an annexationist or imperialist. I was made to feel like Joseph Chamberlain, Bismarck, King Leopold I of the Belgians, or Genghis Khan. To avoid repetition and to assume that this time I may be criticized for other motives, I point out that the motion contains the expression "if the residents of any of these (non-independent) islands so desire it".
I am not a conquistador. I am not an imperialist. I say it again: I am a gentle parliamentarian of Canada trying to express the best intentions toward areas of real concern to this country. I am not interested in a colonial empire for Canada but I am interested in giving or renewing a high priority to an area of the world in which we are uniquely able to be helpful. The communique of the 1966 Canada-Commonwealth Caribbean Conference, Article 23 declared:
In keeping with the intention of the Heads of Government that the consultation instituted at this conference should be continued, it was agreed that a meeting of the governments represented should be held, at a date to be fixed and at an agreed venue in the West Indies for a general discussion of Commonwealth Caribbean-Canada relations and to review progress.
Ten years have passed and no such summit meeting has been heid. I think this is most regrettable. I realize that the Commonwealth Caribbean states have formed or joined other associations, but I am far from convinced that any diminution of the special relationship between our two areas will be advantageous to either.
I would like to see Canada take an initiative on this. Meanwhile a joint committee would serve to signal a rebirth of interest and a renewal of amity on our part.
I have suggested a joint committee because I have the highest regard for a study made six years ago by the foreign affairs committee of the other place. They prepared a valuable report after hearing academics, economists, political leaders, industrialists, businessmen and community leaders. Its recommendations were important, and I believe one of the most important ones was this:
The possibility of constitutional links between Canada and the countries of the Caribbean area should be re-appraised by the Canadian government. This prospect now seems remote, but the Canadian government should be prepared to discuss proposals for closer economic and political association between Canada and countries of the area.
Another, No. 5, is also important.
The excellent and highly competitive rums of the Commonwealth Caribbean should receive as much assistance as possible in the Canadian market. The 1966 agreement to implement labelling regulations went into effect on July 1st, 1969, but does not appear to have led to any dramatic increase in imports. The committee recommends that the Canadian government reassess the effectiveness of this measure and that the mutual advantages to Canada and the Caribbean countries concerned be discussed at the ministerial level with the respective Canadian provinces.
I do not see how anyone could read that statement of the Senate committee and suggest that the Senate is not a useful body. I think in the interests of trade and of the digestive system of Canadian citizens, the emphasis upon the fine quality West Indian rum is well placed. Rum is not the only commodity of importance. There are many products from the West Indies which could be purchased by Canadians. In all of the conferences I described at the beginning of my remarks one of the important issues raised was the question of how we could take advantage of the things they produce which we do not. Fifty years ago Robert Borden said that as we do not produce bananas and sugar we should buy them from the West Indies.
In my lifetime, Mr. Speaker, one of the great national blunders has been the decline of our merchant marine. It would be in our interest to get the shipyards open again and revivify the north-south commerce on the Atlantic seaboard.
These are but some practical considerations and some questions which could be weighed and discussed in an atmosphere of good will by parliamentarians and peoples of the Commonwealth Caribbean and of this Dominion. I offer this as a practical suggestion, Mr. Speaker.
Today a newsman asked me if I did not think it incongruous that we should be discussing the remote possibility of our country being enlarged at a time when people thought it might be diminished. I said that I do not think it will be diminished because I think the same processes of moderate judgment and good will will hold our country together. I would also subscribe to what Mr. Pearson said more than once however: if we have reached the stage in this country that we are completely absorbed in our own affairs and neglect our responsibility to the world, then indeed we might be in grave trouble.
I think good citizens of Canada and good parliamentarians of Canada must embrace the words of John Keats, long, long ago, and describe themselves as those to whom the miseries of the world are misery.
I am glad to submit this motion, Mr. Speaker. While I do not think hon. members opposite were listening, I hope the record will show that this House on this Friday afternoon spent some time directing its attention to a very important part of the world. I urge support of this motion as a gesture of good will to our very, very close and very, very important friends in what I might call the southern commonwealth neighbourhood of this hemisphere.

November 19, 1976

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for the interest he shows in international events as he once was a radio commentator on international affairs, member of the Canada-U.S. and International Political Sciences Association and of the Canadian Institute of International Affairs. He is also the author of several very interesting articles on international affairs. He has also been a member of the UN Canadian Association since his election in 1957. He is a Canadian delegate to the UN General Assembly. So one understands his interests for the international scene because he is a man dedicated to Canada's external affairs.
I do not think it would be necessary to read over motion No. 13. However I want to draw the attention of hon. members on the last sentence which I would like to quote:
-economic and political union of these islands with the Dominion of Canada be negotiated at an early date at the proper constitutional levels.
I am pleased to note that that resolution was tabled on October 20, 1976, that is before the results of the election of November 15 last in the province of Quebec were known. It is strange to see that certain Canadians would seem to want to separate from Canada and that non-Canadians would want to join the most beautiful country in the world, and one sees that non-Canadians from the Turks and Caicos Islands also want, through the hon. member for Hillsborough, to join our beautiful country that we all love and respect so much.
However I would not want my words to be construed as meaning that I am convinced that Quebecers want to separate from Canada. On the contrary, it is now recognized and admitted that the majority of Quebecers strongly want to remain within our confederation made up of a number of provinces and known as Canada. Furthermore, I think it is appropriate to point out the effort of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), a Progressive Conservative, a member of the same party as the hon. member for Hillsborough, who would now want the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to become provinces of Canada.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I would certainly have a personal interest in Canada uniting with those islands as in bad times we might move Parliament to those islands and that might help me avoid flu like I have now, and I would be quite happy besides that. But, seriously speaking-

-as mentioned by the hon. member, this intriguing idea has been discussed in this House before, in May, 1975. The then secretary of state for external affairs had tabled a statement on a similar proposal in April, 1974. Earlier in that year a private member's bill had been introduced by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman). This called attention to a proposed association between Canada and the Turks and Caicos Islands.
The question of a close political relationship between Canada and the Islands in the West Indies has also been raised
West Indies
periodically on earlier occasions. In the statement of the former secretary of state for external affairs just referred to, it was pointed out that the question was given particularly close attention by Sir Robert Borden toward the end of World War I, but since that time there is no record that any Canadian government contemplated such a proposal. Canada has not sought to extend its territory beyond its present borders.
This latest manifestation of a Canadian interest in the Commonwealth Caribbean, nonetheless, deserves careful analysis. It is perhaps understandable that this subject has risen again at this time of year when the annual flow of Canadian visitors southward is getting under way.
Canadian tourism in the Commonwealth Caribbean, which has grown steadily over the years, is one of the long-standing links we have with that area. A very recent official manifestation of Canadian interest was the visit of Mr. Manley, Prime Minister of Jamaica. As you know, he was here in late October and described his visit in glowing terms on return to his capital, Kingston. Hon. members who were present will doubtless remember vividly the very interesting dialogue Mr. Manley had with members of the Standing Committees on External Affairs and National Defence of both Houses and with the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association during an informal meeting on October 28.
Canada's links with Jamaica are important but not less so than with the other and varied members of the Commonwealth Caribbean. These links include important investment and two way trade. There has been a growing immigration program and our common interests are intensified by some shared traditions and parliamentary institutions. Many people in the Commonwealth Caribbean countries have received their education at some level or other in Canada. Some fought in the Canadian Armed Forces during the war. We have links in the field of transportation, particularly air transportation, which help to promote the flow of tourism. Last but by no means least, we have a significant program of development assistance with increasing concentration on the lower income territories.
In the field of trade and aid we have been seeking to replace the old 1925 Canada/West Indies Trade Agreement, as amended by the 1966 Protocol, by a new form of relationship more compatible with the current international economic realities of the Commonwealth Caribbean countries. Two rounds of consultations at the level of senior officials have taken place during the last year and it is hoped that in due course this new relationship can be established. One feature of the discussions to date has been the question of industrial co-operation between Canada and the members of CARICOM, which is the Caribbean Community and Common Market. CARICOM contains two types of members, the independent states of Guyana, Trinidad & Tobago, Jamaica, Barbados and Grenada and also the Associated States which are five territories in the Windward and Leeward Islands. They have complete internal self government but rely on the British for their defence and foreign relations.

November 19, 1976
West Indies
Although these five territories are small and not independent we have been very active in the aid field, and in general are very visible in the region. I think it is true to say we have contributed significantly to their economic progress and we shall continue to do so.
The importance of all these ties is worth emphasizing to show that Canada is playing a significant role in the area and is able to do so without any form of constitutional links with any of these territories. I believe that we can continue to play such a role and the links, for example, constitutional union or absorption, which could result from the motion before us, would in fact have a counter-productive effect on relations which are now of mutual benefit to Canada and the Commonwealth Caribbean.
Mr. Speaker, let us look clearly and frankly at the current circumstances of the Turks and Caicos Islands themselves. In spite of their small population, these islands suffer from the widespread Caribbean problem of too many people supported by too few natural resources. The form of government is that of State Council the majority of whose members are elected, and over which the Governor of the Islands exerts certain powers of control. Although there is some subsistence agriculture in the islands, most foodstuffs have to be imported, as do all manufactured goods.
One of the most important sources of income for the Turks and Caicos islanders is the money earned by the several thousand people of the country who are working elsewhere, particularly in the Bahamas. So far, tourism has developed to only a limited extent, but there remains a potential for considerable expansion. A few Canadians are living in the islands and a greater number have visited them as tourists. It is evident that the people of the Turks and Caicos Islands have a friendly interest in Canada and Canadians and that a number of them were attracted by the idea of constitutional association with Canada.
However, it is one thing to be attracted by a theory and a very different thing when one must consider in depth the practical consequences of such a development. To begin with, the islands are receiving very substantial direct subventions from the British government which work out to approximately $500 per capita per annum. This funding appears to be a basic necessity simply to enable government institutions to function. If the islands were to join in the Canadian Confederation, we would quite naturally seek to raise the basic level of services to the standard expected throughout this country. The primary problem resulting from such an increase in the standard of living in the Turks and Caicos might well be a growing dissatisfaction in other similarly placed territories in the Commonwealth Caribbean that they too could not share in this greater wealth, either inside or indeed while remaining outside Confederation. I suggest that we would find that Canada was being drawn into an intolerable situation whereby we would have at some point to make an artificial distinction and say what was fine for the Turks and Caicos Islands would be unacceptable for other, equally needy, territories. In fact there are several other territories in the Caribbean which could
legitimately claim to have had a longer and closer relationship with Canada than the Turks and Caicos Islands.
However welcome, well-meaning and well-conducted the involvement of an outside power may be in a non-contiguous region, it is nevertheless vulnerable to charges of colonial interference. For Canada to become involved constitutionally with a territory in the region could give rise to a range of difficulties. What, for instance, would be the Canadian government reaction should there be serious local disruptions and a deterioration in the security situation? However pure our motives, remedial action would look very much like colonial repression, and might well be interpreted in this light.
Such links would inevitably arouse suspicions of Canadian motives. In absorbing territory so far from Canada as part of our own country we would inevitably lay ourselves open to charges of unwarranted interference. The general balance of our even handed and carefully developed policies in the area would be upset by this act of constitutional absorption. By this act we would become a Caribbean country and might be drawn into conflicts and affairs of this rather distant region. This could well be embarrassing. In so doing we would endanger our status as a good friend and provider of disinterested development assistance.
We would also be swimming against the independence currents which have been accepted by both Britain and her various Caribbean dependencies. Canada has supported this evolution in various international forums, such as the United Nations General Assembly and at the Commonwealth heads of government meetings.
It would thus appear inconsistent if Canada were to be the nation to re-introduce a foreign element into the Caribbean which could, at its worst, be interpreted as neo-colonialism and, at best, as bringing into being a very unbalanced partnership of interests which could push local economies into disequilibrium.
Let us instead maintain our friendly and responsible approach to the Caribbean as a whole and not jeopardize our reputation by taking on new commitments, the import and extent of which it is impossible to foresee.
As you have noticed, Mr. Speaker, I am having some problems with my voice, so, to conclude, may I say that the reasons given are important enough not to accept the motion.

In other words, I see that my friend, the hon. member for Hillsborough, is trying to counter a certain referendum that might take place in one part of the country with a referendum in an area that is not yet part of the country. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to support the motion proposed by my friend, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). I understand that my hon. friend's constituency now is 20 centimetres deep in snow, that parts of it are without electricity, and that this miserable state of affairs will persist until tomorrow. Under such circumstances there is no doubt that one's thoughts turn to sunny climes, sandy white beaches, the gentle wash of warm water upon them and to the sounds of guitars strumming in the night, and of ice tinkling in glasses. In short, this is the time of year when one might hope that Canada would be a somewhat warmer place.
I think the motion of the hon. member for Hillsborough has been well supported by his speech, which I thought was truly excellent. He put it into an international perspective, and though the speech of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Leblanc) had a pessimistic conclusion, I thought it was a very thoughtful look at the economic factors involved, and he should be complimented for contributing much to the debate. I do not share the hon. member's pessimism, and I hope I will be giving reasoned answers to his reasoned doubts in a few moments.
I represent an area which was formerly represented years ago by that great internationalist, Sir Robert Borden, and when the hon. member for Hillsborough noted that Sir Robert had talked about the two way trade, rum coming up and cod going down, it struck a very responsive note. As a matter of fact it is very likely that the rum cargoes arrived improved by ocean travel. It is not always certain that the cod went the other way increasing in quality as it went, but in any event

November 19, 1976
West Indies
there are two different countries, two different climates, and two different sets of products. They can provide us an opportunity to enjoy sunshine and a different set of living conditions in the winter, and if such a union were ever to come about, it would mean that they could look thousands of miles away knowing that they had friends and that they had opportunities to seek a way of life in the northern hemisphere.
I think my hon. friend has put the emphasis on the approach in the right way. It should be done by a joint committee of parliament, not by a group of bureaucrats. It should be done by people who are versed in the political process because, as the parliamentary secretary has so well noted, as well as the hon. member for Hillsborough, we have to be careful of any approach which is made. As the hon. member for Hillsborough said, we cannot go as conquistadors. I cannot imagine him going as a conquistador in any event. We cannot go there as spoilers or exploiters.
If we were ever asked there to assume some federal partnership with these people, we would have to be very careful to avoid the mistakes which have plagued other parts of the West Indies, the mistakes which give rise to racial tensions. For example, we should be very careful to ensure that a reasonable part of the ownership of resource facilities remains in local hands so that they would not feel that a group had descended upon them and, in the guise of friendship, taken over their wonderful part of the world and suddenly turned them into mere employees. We have to be very careful to avoid something like that, and that would probably involve a much greater share of government participation in any investment than perhaps ordinarily would be the case.
I think also that if there is to be any joint committee at work in this field, we should show our willingness to set up such a joint committee by adopting the motion of the hon. member for Hillsborough, but I would also like to see coming back to us before we venture anywhere further from that a council statement, as I gather the parliamentary secretary noted that their form of government is by council. There should be some statement by the people in the Turks, by the people in the Caicos and by the people on any other island in the British West Indies who would be interested in union with Canada so that we would know that there is an opinion from there before any Canadian ever goes near there or, for that matter, before they come anywhere near Canada.
In short, I think if we took steps such as that, we could go to them as friends showing interest, we could argue about all the good things Canada could do for them, and I am sure they would be able to argue about the good things they could do for us.
One obvious and very early step would be to build an international airport on any island which enters into a liaison or union with us, and in that development Canadian technology would surely have its role. In recent years some of us have been to Colombo, Sri Lanka-the former Ceylon-and seen a great international airport there. It makes the one a few miles away, the Ottawa International Airport, look very old fash-
[Mr. McCleave.J
ioned indeed. It was the gift of Canadian technology which made that great airport in Colombo possible.

If I can sound chauvinistic just for a moment in the Nova Scotia chauvinistic sense, any islands which do take advantage of this wedding proposal should naturally find that provincially they would become a part of Nova Scotia and educationally, probably, a part of the Halifax county school system, which indeed is a rather good school system.
In suggesting that his colleagues not support the motion, the parliamentary secretary suggested that there might be discrimination among those small islands. He presented his reasoning as well as he could, and he is a very forceful fellow when he gets going, but I do not think that is so. The motion presented by the hon. member for Hillsborough gives an opportunity to small places which otherwise would not likely be terribly interested in voting on this subject unless they knew that there would be some interest or sympathy at the other end of the line for their position. So, in short, I have to say to the hon. member for Laurier that we would not be thwarting independence by adopting the motion.
If we deny this motion, we forbid or prevent those people from a freedom of choice, that choice being whether to join us as Canadians or not. To me that seems to be a discrimination, even though it might seem like a discrimination in reverse. As small islands they probably would not feel particularly fitted for independence. I gather that to be so, and there would be thousands or tens of thousands living on an island who would find it very difficult to imagine such groups as nations, though I suppose several of them banded together might be able to give themselves the feeling of being a nation. But to imagine themselves as part of a much larger country, one of the greatest countries of the world, surely should not be beyond their comprehension, and perhaps it would be something they would want.
I have to stand corrected. It is not the riding of the hon. member for Hillsborough which is inundated with all that snow I mentioned earlier. His constituency has so far missed the storm, and I suppose by sending me the note he did, the hon. member just wants to prove that he represents his people well and will not allow them to suffer the affliction of a major snowstorm.
In any event, I thank the House for its attention. I thank the hon. member for giving me an opportunity to support his motion. I cannot see any harm coming out of it. I hope it starts off a vigorous debate both here and in the West Indies. After all, eventually it will be a matter on which all sides will have their say, and I am pleased to support what seems to be a constructive idea.

Mr. Speaker, as surprising as it may seem, since the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) has introduced the motion which we are debating today, and since the more or less convincing and persuading intervention of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), I have had the opportunity to conduct certain in-depth studies on the subject of this afternoon's debate and 1 have come to the conclusion that the motion we are considering contains a proposition which could, in spite of its superficial interest- that is warm sands and what not-cause serious damage to the relations between Canada and the West Indies if it were passed.
Indeed, the West Indies has had special ties with Canada for many years and these ties have been strengthened in a very human way by the fact that thousands of Canadian tourists visit that country every year.
The relationship is generally relaxed and pleasant and I feel that we must ensure that we do not introduce any new perturbing element. If, like my hon. friend from Hillsborough suggests, in his capacity as expert on foreign policy, we name a joint committee of the Senate and the House to study the question with a view to creating a political partnership, we could very well introduce such a perturbing element.
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be much support to your right this afternoon. I also feel that we should reevaluate in a very pragmatic way the probable repercussions of a union between Canada and one or maybe several smaller non independent countries of the West Indies.
Let us look first at the economic results-though the hon. member for Winnipeg-North Center said a while ago that they were out of the question-precisely to present arguments with a view to preventing that study which, to my mind, because of present circumstances, is absolutely useless and, to say the least, superfluous.
One must not forget that most of those territories are relatively underdeveloped economically; they would need massive injections of Canadian capital to reach the level of economic activity that should be expected of them. Those injections could bring greater results in the sector associated with the construction of facilities connected with tourism, because
West Indies
eventual investments would be encouraged by the prospect of Canadians travelling to that new part of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? I was wondering if the hon. member-

speechtext:
I will be in a position to answer the question outside the House.
Even though on the face of it such investments in tourist facilities may seem attractive, the overall impact must be studied within the context on the total area, like everything else that involves the Commonwealth Caribbeans. Increased investments and tourist trade in a given area would most likely deprive other countries of the Commonwealth Caribbeans of their revenues from those sources. This would lead to increased unemployment levels and lower living standards in those other countries. Such is certainly not the aim pursued by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). As far as investments are concerned, massive imports of Canadian money could go to agriculture or even to low cost manufacturing industries in the proposed new Canadian island, considering the easier access to our market. This could dry up capital for other Caribbean countries, restraining their traditional share of the Canadian market. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the will and ability of those countries to maintain their level of exports to Canada could be affected. In my view, this tends to show that from every economic, trade, commercial and investment aspect, any advantage would be more than offset by the disadvantages.
And since the time is going so fast, I would state in conclusion that although I am not against those who would join in a greater Canadian family, in the circumstances I referred to before, Canada must first attempt to keep what she has, and keep everything! I therefore ask the government, and especially Parliament to work toward that goal, giving fair treatment to every Canadian, and giving a chance to remain Canadian to those who, although a majority of them wish to remain so, unfortunately or otherwise voted last Monday to elect a separatist party.
